title: Start here: how IELTS Reading works
what: The Reading test has 3 passages and 40 questions. You get 60 minutes in total. There is no extra time to copy your answers, so you must write them on the answer sheet as you go. This note gives you one method that works for every question type.

steps.do: Skim the passage for one minute. Note the paragraph letters and what each is about. If a paragraph has no letter, label it yourself.
steps.why: A quick map means you know where to look later, so you do not read everything twice.

steps.do: Read the question and underline the keywords: names, numbers, dates and unusual nouns.
steps.why: These words usually stay the same in the passage, so they are easy to spot.

steps.do: Predict the paraphrase (the same idea in different words). Think of other ways to say the important words.
steps.why: The passage rarely uses the same words as the question. Knowing synonyms helps you find the right sentence.

steps.do: Find the keyword or its paraphrase in the passage. Then read the sentence before and after it.
steps.why: The answer is often next to the keyword, not on it. One extra sentence stops careless mistakes.

steps.do: Confirm your answer. Point to the exact words in the passage that prove it.
steps.why: If you cannot point to a line, you are guessing. A guess from memory or opinion is often wrong.

steps.do: Spend about 20 minutes on each passage. Move on when a question takes too long, and come back later.
steps.why: Each passage has the same number of marks. One hard question must not steal time from easy ones.

steps.do: Never leave a blank. Write your best guess before you finish.
steps.why: There is no penalty for a wrong answer, so a guess can only help you.

demo.prompt: Statement: Supermarkets started buying the bakery's bread in 2001. Is this TRUE, FALSE or NOT GIVEN?
demo.text: A: The Greenfield bakery opened in 1975 with only two ovens. Over the next twenty years, it grew into the largest employer in the village. B: In 2001 the owners began selling bread to supermarkets. Sales rose sharply, but the bakery still makes most of its loaves by hand.

moves.say: I skim the passage first. Paragraph A is about the bakery's start. Paragraph B is about a change in 2001, so I label them and move on.
moves.mark: In 2001 the owners

moves.say: I underline the keywords in the statement: supermarkets and 2001. The year is a number, so it is easy to spot in the text.
I predict a paraphrase. 'Supermarkets started buying' might be written as 'began selling bread to supermarkets'.
moves.mark: began selling bread to supermarkets

moves.say: I find 2001 in paragraph B and read the sentences around it. The sentence after it talks about sales, so I keep reading.
moves.mark: In 2001 the owners began selling bread to supermarkets

moves.say: I confirm with a line. 'Began selling bread to supermarkets' says the same as the statement, so I answer TRUE.
moves.mark: began selling bread to supermarkets

demo.answer: TRUE. The line 'began selling bread to supermarkets' says the same thing as the statement.

practice.prompt: Sam is answering a True / False / Not Given question. Which step did he skip? Use the five steps to decide.
practice.text: Sam skimmed the passage and labelled both paragraphs. He underlined 'supermarkets' in the question and predicted that 'began selling' would appear. He found the sentence in paragraph B and read the sentences around it. He wrote TRUE and moved on, without pointing to the exact words that prove it.
options: Find it and read around it
practice.why: Step 5 asks you to point to the exact words that prove your answer. Sam found the right sentence but never pointed to the words that prove TRUE. He should have checked them before writing.

practice.prompt: Priya's question asks whether rent rose. Which step did she skip? Use the five steps to decide.
practice.text: Priya found the word 'rent' in the second paragraph and wrote 'it rose' straight away. She did not read the sentence before or after it. The next sentence said the rent had fallen, so her answer was wrong.
options: Find it and read around it
practice.answer: Find it and read around it
practice.why: Step 4 says the answer is often next to the keyword, not on it. Priya read only the keyword line. The sentence after it showed the rent had fallen, which changes the answer.
practice.evidence: The next sentence said the rent had fallen

tricks: Most gap-filling and True/False types follow the order of the passage. If question 5 is in paragraph B, question 6 will be later in paragraph B or after it.
Do the easy question types first, such as short gap-fills. Leave long matching tasks until you have time to think.
Check the word limit in the instructions. 'No more than two words' means three words is wrong, even if the idea is right.
Copy words from the passage exactly. Do not change the form of a word unless the sentence needs it.
traps: Spelling counts. A correct answer with a wrong spelling gets no mark, so copy the word letter by letter from the passage.
Do not use your own knowledge. The test only asks what this passage says, so answer from the text.
Do not stop at the first matching word. The same word can appear in two places, and only one place answers the question. Read around it.
Do not spend more than a minute stuck on one question. Mark it, move on, and return if you have time.

signals.means: Paraphrase means saying the same thing in different words. The question says 'prices rose' and the passage says 'prices climbed'.
Different words, same idea. The question says 'caused delays' and the passage says 'led to delays'.
Simple swaps like this are very common. The question says 'began in 1990' and the passage says 'started in 1990'.
A short word can become a longer phrase. 'Many people' can appear as 'a great number of people'.

checklist: Do I know that paraphrase means saying the same thing in different words?
Did I check the word limit before I wrote my answer?
Can I point to the line in the passage that proves my answer?
Is my spelling copied exactly from the passage?
Have I filled in every answer, even the ones I guessed?

title: True / False / Not Given
what: You get a statement about the passage. You decide if the passage agrees with it (True), says the opposite (False), or does not say (Not Given). The question is not 'is this correct in real life?'. The question is 'what does this passage say?'.

steps.do: Read the statement and underline the keywords. Think of other words that mean the same thing.
steps.why: The passage will use different words, so you need to know what to look for.

steps.do: Find the part of the passage that talks about the same topic. Questions follow the order of the passage.
steps.why: This stops you searching the whole text and saves time.

steps.do: Read the whole paragraph around that part, not just one sentence.
steps.why: A later sentence can change the meaning, for example with 'however' or 'but'.

steps.do: Ask: can I point to a line that says the same thing? If yes, the answer is True.
steps.why: True means the passage agrees. It may use different words, but the meaning is the same.

steps.do: If not, ask: can I point to a line that says the opposite? If yes, the answer is False.
steps.why: False means the passage clearly disagrees. You need real words that contradict the statement.

steps.do: If you find neither after reading the whole paragraph, the answer is Not Given.
steps.why: Not Given means the passage is silent about this idea. Silence is not the same as disagreement.

steps.do: Check every small word in the statement against the passage before you choose.
steps.why: One wrong word, such as 'all' or 'only', can turn a True answer into False or Not Given.

demo.prompt: Statement: The company's boats were built in Norway. Is this TRUE, FALSE or NOT GIVEN?
demo.text: A: The Harbour Ferry Company started in 1962 with one boat. By 1980 it ran six boats across the bay every day. B: Fares rose in 1995, and many older passengers complained about the cost. Two new boats were ordered in 2010. The company has never said how many passengers use its summer service.

moves.say: I underline the keywords: boats, built, Norway. The passage uses the word boats, so I look for it in the text.
moves.mark: boats

moves.say: The topic is the company's boats. Paragraph A is about them, so I look there first.
moves.mark: The Harbour Ferry Company started in 1962 with one boat.

moves.say: I read the whole paragraph, not one sentence. Nothing in A says where the boats were built.
moves.mark: By 1980 it ran six boats across the bay every day.

moves.say: Can I point to a line that says the boats were built in Norway? I scan the boat sentences, such as the 1962 one. None of them says that.
moves.mark: The Harbour Ferry Company started in 1962 with one boat.

moves.say: Is there a line that says the opposite, such as built somewhere else? I check the boat sentences again. No line says that either.
I find neither a matching line nor an opposite one. So the answer is NOT GIVEN. Silence is not disagreement.
I check the detail 'Norway' against the passage. It is not there, so the answer stays NOT GIVEN.

demo.answer: NOT GIVEN. No line says the boats were built in Norway, and no line says they were not.

practice.prompt: Statement: The bakery bakes its bread before six o'clock every morning. Use the steps: find the line that says it, then confirm with the exact words. Is this TRUE, FALSE or NOT GIVEN?
practice.text: Maya's bakery opened in 2001 on Mill Road. It sells bread, cakes and seasonal pies. Every morning, the owner bakes the bread before six o'clock. Customers can order birthday cakes by phone, but not online.
practice.why: Step 4: the line 'the owner bakes the bread before six o'clock' says the same thing. 'Every morning' matches the statement too. So the answer is TRUE.
practice.evidence: the owner bakes the bread before six o'clock

practice.prompt: Statement: All of the library's books are for children. Use the steps, and check every small word before you choose. Is this TRUE, FALSE or NOT GIVEN?
practice.text: The school library has 4,000 books, and most of them are for children. Students can borrow up to five books at a time. Only the head teacher can order new adult books. The library is open until four o'clock on weekdays.
practice.why: Step 7: the small word 'All' is the problem. The passage says 'most', not 'all', so the line contradicts the statement. The answer is FALSE, not TRUE.
practice.evidence: most of them are for children

tricks: Use this order every time: first look for a line that agrees (True), then for a line that says the opposite (False), and only then choose Not Given.
The answers follow the order of the passage. Use the place of the question before as a starting point for the next one.
Watch for one wrong word. If a statement is nearly right but one detail is different, it is False or Not Given, not True.
If the topic is in the passage but this exact detail is missing, that is Not Given. The detail has to be written, not guessed.
traps: Using your own knowledge. Even if you know the statement is true in real life, answer only from the passage.
Choosing False when the passage is silent. Silent means Not Given. False needs words that say the opposite.
Stopping at the first matching keyword. The same word may appear again later with a different meaning. Read the whole paragraph.
Ignoring small words. 'Always', 'only', 'all' and 'never' are very strong. Check the passage supports that strength, not just a weaker version.

example.text: The town library opened in 1952 and has grown steadily since then. Most visitors are students who use the quiet reading rooms. The library offers free internet to all members. It does not lend laptops, though staff say this may change next year.
example.question: The library lends laptops to students. (True / False / Not Given)
walk: Keywords: lends, laptops, students. 'Lends' may appear as 'lend'.
The last sentence is about laptops, so we read it closely.
The text says the library 'does not lend laptops'. That is the opposite of the statement.
So the answer is False. If the text had never mentioned laptops at all, it would be Not Given.

signals.means: 100 per cent. If the passage says 'most' or 'many', then 'all' is False.
Very strong words. Check the passage really says the same, not something weaker.
Possible, not certain. A statement that says 'will' is not the same as the passage saying 'may'.
Quantity words. 'Most' and 'some' are different amounts.

checklist: Can I point to the exact line that proves True or False?
If I chose Not Given, did I read the whole paragraph and find nothing?
Did I check small words like all, only, never and always?
Did I answer from the passage, not from what I already know?

title: Yes / No / Not Given
what: This works like True / False / Not Given, but the statement is about the writer's opinion or claims, not facts. You decide if the writer agrees (Yes), disagrees (No), or does not say (Not Given).

steps.do: Read the statement and underline the keywords. Remember it is about what the writer thinks.
steps.why: You are looking for the writer's view, not a fact in the text.

steps.do: Find the part of the passage about the same topic. The questions follow the order of the passage.
steps.why: This keeps your search short and in the right place.

steps.do: Read the whole paragraph. Look for words that show opinion, such as 'believes', 'argues' or 'it seems'.
steps.why: Opinion words tell you the writer is giving a view, not just a fact.

steps.do: Ask: does the writer clearly agree with the statement? If yes, answer Yes.
steps.why: Yes means the writer's view matches the statement, even if the words are different.

steps.do: Ask: does the writer clearly disagree? If yes, answer No.
steps.why: No means the writer's view is the opposite of the statement.

steps.do: If the writer gives no view on this idea, answer Not Given.
steps.why: Not Given means the writer is silent on this point. Do not guess their opinion.

steps.do: Check who is speaking. Make sure the opinion belongs to the writer, not someone else.
steps.why: Passages often quote experts. The question asks only about the writer.

demo.prompt: Statement: The writer believes cars should be banned from city centres. Is this YES, NO or NOT GIVEN?
demo.text: A: Some people think cars should be banned from city centres. Dr Patel argues that this would reduce pollution and noise. B: The writer disagrees with a total ban, because many people still need a car to reach work. Buses and taxis, however, should be given priority on the busiest roads.

moves.say: I underline the keywords: writer, cars, banned, city centres. This question is about the writer's view, not anyone else's.
moves.mark: banned from city centres

moves.say: I find the topic in paragraph A. It is about banning cars, so I look near it for the writer's own view.
moves.mark: should be banned from city centres

moves.say: I read the whole paragraph. I look for opinion words such as 'argues' and 'disagrees', and I note who says each one.
moves.mark: Dr Patel argues that this would reduce pollution and noise.

moves.say: Does the writer clearly agree? The writer does not say cars should be banned, so the answer is not YES.
moves.mark: The writer disagrees with a total ban

moves.say: Does the writer clearly disagree? Yes, the writer disagrees with a total ban. So the answer is NO.
moves.mark: The writer disagrees with a total ban

moves.say: Before I answer, I check who is speaking. Dr Patel's view does not count, because the question asks only about the writer.
moves.mark: Dr Patel argues that this would reduce pollution and noise.

demo.answer: NO. The writer disagrees with a total ban. Dr Patel's view does not count.

practice.prompt: Statement: The writer thinks libraries have become community centres. Use the steps: find the writer's own view, not a critic's. Is this YES, NO or NOT GIVEN?
practice.text: A: Libraries are not just places for books any more. The writer believes they are now community centres. B: Many libraries run computer classes and baby groups. Some critics say this distracts from reading, but the writer rejects that view.
practice.why: Step 4: the line 'The writer believes they are now community centres' agrees with the statement. The critics are not the writer, so their view does not change the answer.
practice.evidence: The writer believes they are now community centres.

practice.prompt: Statement: The writer thinks the high street will decline within ten years. Use the steps, and check who holds the view. Is this YES, NO or NOT GIVEN?
practice.text: A: Professor Lin says that the high street will decline sharply within ten years. She bases this on sales figures from the last decade. B: The writer describes three shops that opened this year, and says the local council is pleased with them. The writer does not say what the future holds for the high street.
practice.why: Step 7: the decline view belongs to Professor Lin, a quoted expert, not the writer. Step 6: the writer says nothing about the future, so the answer is NOT GIVEN.
practice.evidence: The writer does not say what the future holds for the high street.

tricks: Use the same three-way test as True / False / Not Given: agree, the opposite, or silent.
Look for opinion words like 'argues', 'claims', 'believes', 'suggests' and 'it seems'. They show where views are given.
Look at the writer's last sentence in a paragraph. It often gives their own conclusion.
Be careful when a statement uses strong words like 'must' or 'always'. The writer may only say 'should' or 'often'.
traps: Mixing up another person's view with the writer's view. If the text says 'Dr Lee argues...', that is Dr Lee, not the writer, unless the writer agrees.
Choosing No when the writer is simply silent. Silent is Not Given. No needs the writer to say the opposite.
Using your own opinion. Even if you agree with the statement, answer only what the writer says.
Stopping at the first keyword. The writer may change their view later with 'however'. Read the whole paragraph.

example.text: Many people say that working from home is always better for staff. In the writer's view, offices still matter. Working from home suits some jobs, but teams often solve problems faster when they meet in person. Some companies now ask staff to visit the office twice a week.
example.question: The writer thinks working from home is better for every worker. (Yes / No / Not Given)
example.evidence: In the writer's view, offices still matter
walk: Keywords: working from home, better, every worker.
The statement is about the writer's view, so we look for the writer.
The text says 'In the writer's view, offices still matter' and that home working only suits some jobs. That is the opposite of 'better for every worker'.
So the answer is No. The opinion at the start ('Many people say...') belongs to other people, not the writer.

signals.means: Someone is giving a view. Check who it is: the writer or another person.
A softer opinion. The writer is not completely sure.
Advice or a strong view. 'Should' is weaker than 'must'.
The view may change. Read on before you decide.

checklist: Is the opinion in the passage the writer's, not someone else's?
Can I point to the line where the writer agrees or disagrees?
If I chose Not Given, did I read the whole paragraph and find no view?
Did I answer from the passage, not from my own opinion?

title: Multiple choice
what: You read a question and choose the best answer from A, B, C or D. Sometimes you must choose more than one answer. The wrong answers are written to look tempting, so you must prove the right one and remove the others.

steps.do: Read the question stem first, before you look at the options. The stem is the question or the start of the sentence.
steps.why: If you read the options first, you may be fooled by a nice-sounding wrong answer.

steps.do: Underline the keywords in the stem. Find that part of the passage. Questions follow the order of the passage.
steps.why: This takes you straight to the right paragraph.

steps.do: Read the passage around the keyword carefully. Do not look at the options yet.
steps.why: Understanding the passage first helps you decide without being influenced by the options.

steps.do: Read all the options. Cross out any that are wrong, and think of a reason for each.
steps.why: A reason makes sure you remove options for a good cause, not a feeling.

steps.do: Choose the option that matches the passage in meaning, even if the words are different.
steps.why: The right answer is usually a paraphrase, not a copy of the passage.

steps.do: Check your choice against the passage once more. Can you point to the proof?
steps.why: A final check catches careless mistakes.

steps.do: If you must pick more than one answer, choose exactly the number asked. Their order does not matter.
steps.why: Choosing too many or too few answers loses marks.

demo.prompt: What is the main benefit of machine-made lenses, according to the passage? A. Workers train for seven years B. Machines cut production time in half C. Photographers prefer machine lenses because the edges are softer D. Machine lenses are always better than hand-ground ones
demo.text: Lenses in old cameras were ground by hand. The workers who made them often trained for seven years. Today most lenses are made by machines, which cut production time in half. Some photographers still prefer hand-ground lenses because they say the images have softer edges.

moves.say: I read the question first: what is the main benefit of machine-made lenses? I do not look at the options yet.
I underline 'machine-made' and 'benefit'. The machine sentence is the third one, so I go there.
moves.mark: Today most lenses are made by machines

moves.say: I read around that sentence. It says machines cut production time in half. I still do not look at the options.
moves.mark: which cut production time in half

moves.say: Now I read the options and cross out the wrong ones. A is true but not asked: it is about hand-making, not machines.
C is half right. 'Softer edges' is in the passage, but some photographers prefer hand-ground lenses for that reason, not machine ones.
D is too extreme. 'Always better' is far stronger than anything the passage says about quality.
Only B is left, and it matches the passage in meaning. The benefit is speed.
I check B against the passage. The line 'cut production time in half' proves it.
moves.mark: cut production time in half

moves.say: The question asks for one answer, so I choose only B.

demo.answer: B. Machines cut production time in half, which is the benefit the passage gives.

practice.prompt: The Oakwood Trust planted trees in 2019. Why did it plant mostly oak trees? Use the steps to find the line that proves your answer. A. They were cheaper than other trees B. They grow well in the local clay soil C. Volunteers liked watering them most D. They survived better than every other kind
practice.text: The Oakwood Trust planted 300 trees in 2019. Most of them were oaks, because oaks grow well in the local clay soil. Volunteers watered the young trees each week for three summers. By 2024, nearly all of the trees had survived.
options: A. They were cheaper than other trees
B. They grow well in the local clay soil
C. Volunteers liked watering them most
D. They survived better than every other kind
practice.answer: B. They grow well in the local clay soil
practice.why: Step 2 finds the 'why' sentence. It says oaks grow well in the local clay soil. A is not in the text, C is not stated, and D is too extreme.
practice.evidence: oaks grow well in the local clay soil

practice.prompt: Why did Ella hire two bakers? Use the steps. Cross out each wrong option and give a reason. A. The lemon cake sells out most days B. The cafe could open earlier C. Ella enjoys meeting her regular customers D. The cafe is famous across the whole country
practice.text: Ella opened a small cafe in May. It is famous for its lemon cake, which sells out most days. She hired two bakers so the cafe could open earlier. Ella says the best part is meeting her regular customers.
options: A. The lemon cake sells out most days
B. The cafe could open earlier
C. Ella enjoys meeting her regular customers
D. The cafe is famous across the whole country
practice.answer: B. The cafe could open earlier
practice.why: A and C are true but not asked: the cake and meeting customers are facts, not the reason for the bakers. D is too extreme. The line 'so the cafe could open earlier' gives the reason: B.
practice.evidence: She hired two bakers so the cafe could open earlier.

tricks: Wrong options are often true but not asked. They are real facts from the passage, but they do not answer this question.
Another common wrong option is half right: the first half matches the passage but the second half is wrong. Read the whole option.
Be careful with options that are too extreme, with words like 'always', 'all' or 'never'. The passage rarely says things that strongly.
When you pick two or three answers, the order you write them does not matter.
traps: Choosing an option because it contains words copied from the passage. Copied words are often a trick. Check the meaning instead.
Choosing an option because it is true in real life. Answer only from the passage.
Reading only one sentence. The answer often needs the sentence before or after as well.
Picking more or fewer answers than the question asks. Check the number in the instructions.

example.text: Maya started cycling to work to save money. After a month she noticed she felt more awake in meetings. She also found she was spending less on fuel than she expected. By the end of the year she had saved enough for a holiday.
example.question: Why did Maya start cycling to work? A. to feel more awake  B. to save money  C. to buy a holiday  D. to spend less on fuel
example.evidence: started cycling to work to save money
walk: Keywords: why, start cycling. The stem asks for the reason she started.
The passage says she 'started cycling to work to save money'.
A is true but not asked: she felt more awake later, as a result, not as a reason to start.
C and D are also later results, not the reason she began. So the answer is B.

signals.means: The option is a fact from the passage but does not answer this question.
The start of the option matches the passage but the end does not.
Words like always, all and never are stronger than what the passage says.

checklist: Did I read the stem before the options?
Can I give a reason for every option I crossed out?
Does my answer match the meaning of the passage, not only the words?
Did I choose exactly the number of answers the question asks for?

title: Short-answer questions
what: You get a question and write a short answer from the passage. The instructions give a word limit, such as NO MORE THAN THREE WORDS. Your answer must come from the passage and stay inside that limit.

steps.do: Read the word limit in the instructions first. Write it at the top of the page if that helps.
steps.why: An answer over the limit gets no mark, even if the idea is right.

steps.do: Read the question. Look at the question word: who, when, where, what or how many.
steps.why: The question word tells you what kind of answer to look for.

steps.do: Underline the keywords in the question, such as names, places and unusual nouns.
steps.why: These words usually stay the same in the passage, so they are easy to find.

steps.do: Find the keywords in the passage. Questions follow the order of the passage, so keep moving forward.
steps.why: This keeps your search short and stops you reading the text twice.

steps.do: Read the sentence around the keywords. Find the word or words that answer the question.
steps.why: The answer is often next to the keyword, not on it.

steps.do: Copy the answer exactly as it is written. Do not change the form of any word.
steps.why: Changing 'teacher' to 'teachers' can lose the mark.

steps.do: Count your words and check the limit. Check your spelling against the passage.
steps.why: A wrong spelling or one word too many gets no mark.

tricks: Match the question word to the answer type. Who is a person, when is a date or time, where is a place, and how many is a number.
A number counts as one word. '1952' is one word, and 'twenty' is one word.
Your answer is the missing piece of information, not a repeat of the question. Use the question's words to find the place in the passage, then copy the answer from beside them.
If your answer is longer than the limit, cut small words. Keep the key words and drop only small ones, for example 'the' before a noun.
traps: Going over the word limit. 'NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS' means three words is wrong, so cut it down.
Changing the word. Copy the form in the passage, not the form you think sounds better.
Writing an answer of the wrong type, such as a place when the question asks 'when'. Check the question word again.
Choosing a keyword match that answers a different question. Read the whole sentence before you copy anything.

example.text: The harbour museum opened in 1998. It holds more than 300 old maps and models of ships. Visitors can join a guided tour every Saturday morning. Entry is free for children under twelve.
example.question: When can visitors join a guided tour? Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS.
walk: The word limit is two words. The question word 'when' asks for a day or time.
Keywords: guided tour. They appear in the third sentence.
The text says 'every Saturday morning'. That is three words, which is over the limit.
Cut the small word 'every'. 'Saturday morning' is two words, copied exactly, so it is correct.

signals.means: Look for a person or group, such as a name, a job or 'the researchers'.
Look for a date, a year, a day or a time of day.
Look for a place, such as a town, a country or 'the north coast'.
Look for a number or an amount. A number counts as one word.

checklist: Did I read the word limit before I wrote my answer?
Does my answer match the question word (who, when, where, how many)?
Did I copy the words exactly and check the spelling?
Did I count the words and stay inside the limit?

demo.prompt: When does the story hour take place? Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS.
demo.text: The Moorfield Library was built in 1908 with money from a local mill owner. It has a reading room with tall windows and about 12,000 books. Children can join the story hour every Thursday afternoon, and it is free. Families must book a place by phone first.

moves.say: I read the limit first: NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS. I write it at the top of my page so I do not go over.
I see the question word 'when'. So I look for a day or a time, not a place or a name.
I underline the keyword: story hour. It is the thing the question asks about, so I look for it in the passage.
I scan the passage for 'story hour'. It is in the third sentence, so I go there and read it.
moves.mark: Children can join the story hour every Thursday afternoon, and it is free.

moves.say: I read the time: after 'every' there is a day and a part of the day. That is my answer.
moves.mark: every Thursday afternoon

moves.say: I copy the words exactly: Thursday afternoon, with the same capital T as the passage.
moves.mark: Thursday afternoon

moves.say: Thursday afternoon is two words, so it is within the limit. I check the spelling against the passage.
moves.mark: Thursday afternoon

practice.prompt: How many lifeguards watch the pool at weekends? Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER. Use the steps: find the question word, the keywords, then the sentence with the answer.
practice.text: The Cresswell Pool opens at 8 am every day in summer. At weekends, five lifeguards watch the pool, while only three work on weekdays. Children under eight must always be with an adult. Swimming lessons are held in the mornings.
practice.why: Step 5: the keyword is 'weekends', and the sentence says 'At weekends, five lifeguards watch the pool'. The number three is for weekdays, so it is the wrong answer. The answer is five.
practice.evidence: At weekends, five lifeguards watch the pool

moves.say: I read the sentence after 'Finally', which matches box 3. The pulp is spread across a long wire screen, so box 3 is screen.
moves.mark: spread across a long wire screen

moves.say: I check the arrows: chips, pulp, screen. Each gap is one word and within the limit.

practice.prompt: Diagram (a flow chart, left to right): Box 1: flour, water and salt are mixed → Box 2: the [gap] rests for two hours → Box 3: loaves are baked in a hot oven. Write ONE WORD ONLY for the gap. Use the steps.
practice.text: Bread is made in three stages at the local bakery. First, the baker mixes flour, water and salt into a smooth dough. Then the dough rests for two hours, which lets it rise slowly. Finally, the loaves are baked in a hot oven for forty minutes.
practice.why: Step 4: 'Then' marks stage two, and the passage says 'the dough rests for two hours'. The gap is a noun that comes before 'rests', and 'dough' is the word the passage uses.
practice.evidence: Then the dough rests for two hours

practice.prompt: Diagram (a flow chart, left to right): Box 1: olives are crushed into a paste → Box 2: the paste is [gap] slowly for thirty minutes → Box 3: oil is separated from the water. Write ONE WORD ONLY for the gap. Use the steps, and check the verb form.
practice.text: Olive oil is produced in three stages at the Vale estate. First, the olives are crushed into a paste, which takes about an hour. The paste is then stirred slowly for thirty minutes, so that small drops of oil can join together. Finally, a machine separates the oil from the water.
practice.why: Steps 3 and 5: the gap is a verb after 'is', and the middle stage says the paste is 'stirred slowly for thirty minutes'. 'Crushed' is the box 1 action, not box 2, so it is wrong.
practice.evidence: The paste is then stirred slowly for thirty minutes

title: Matching headings
what: You get a list of headings and a passage split into lettered paragraphs. You choose the heading that gives the main idea of each paragraph. There are more headings than paragraphs, and each heading is used only once.

steps.do: Read the list of headings first. Underline the key words in each one.
steps.why: You know what to look for before you read, which saves time.

steps.do: Look at the example, if there is one. Cross out that heading, because it is already used.
steps.why: Headings can be used only once, so this removes one choice.

steps.do: Read the first and last sentence of the paragraph. These often state the main idea and the conclusion.
steps.why: A paragraph usually opens with its main idea and ends by closing it.

steps.do: Skim the middle quickly. Ask: what is this whole paragraph about, not just one detail?
steps.why: A heading is the main idea of the whole paragraph, not one small fact.

steps.do: Choose the heading with the same meaning, in different words. Start with the easiest paragraphs.
steps.why: Headings are paraphrases, which means the same idea in other words. Easy ones first leaves fewer choices.

steps.do: Cross out each heading as you use it. Keep going until the paragraphs are done.
steps.why: Each cross removes a choice, so the hard paragraphs get easier.

steps.do: Check each answer: does the heading cover the whole paragraph, not only one sentence?
steps.why: A heading that fits only a small detail is a wrong answer.

demo.prompt: Headings: i) What happened to the railway line after it closed. ii) Steam engines and the coal they carried. iii) Who uses the new walking path. iv) Plans for new trees and wildlife along the route. v) The history of the town's bus station. Match paragraphs A, B and C to a heading each. Two headings are not used.
demo.text: A: The railway through Hale Valley closed in 1968. Steam engines had pulled coal wagons along the line for decades. After the closure, the track lay unused, and weeds grew between the rails for thirty years. B: Walkers and cyclists now use the new path every day. Many say it is the safest way to reach school. Local cafes have also reported more customers since the path opened. C: The council plans to plant two hundred trees along the route. Birds have already returned to the bushes near the track. Wildlife experts expect the area to look very different by 2030.

moves.say: I read the five headings first. I underline the key words in each one, so I know what to look for.
This task has no example, so there is no heading to cross out yet. I go to the passage.
I read the first sentence of A. It tells me the railway closed, so this paragraph is about the line.
moves.mark: The railway through Hale Valley closed in 1968.

moves.say: I read the last sentence of A. It says the track was left unused, which supports the same main idea.
moves.mark: After the closure, the track lay unused, and weeds grew between the rails for thirty years.

moves.say: I see that B's first sentence gives the main idea: people use the path.
moves.mark: Walkers and cyclists now use the new path every day.

moves.say: I see that C's first sentence names the council's plan. I think that is where its main idea starts.
moves.mark: The council plans to plant two hundred trees along the route.

moves.say: I skim the middle of A. This sentence is a detail about the past, not the whole paragraph.
moves.mark: Steam engines had pulled coal wagons along the line for decades.

moves.say: I skim the middle of C. It supports the wildlife idea, so the main idea stays the same.
moves.mark: Birds have already returned to the bushes near the track.

moves.say: I think A is about the line closing and lying unused. Heading i says that in other words, so A gets i.
moves.mark: The railway through Hale Valley closed in 1968.

moves.say: I think B is about people using the path. Heading iii matches, so B gets iii.
moves.mark: Walkers and cyclists now use the new path every day.

moves.say: I think C is about plans for trees and wildlife. Heading iv matches, so C gets iv.
moves.mark: The council plans to plant two hundred trees along the route.

moves.say: I cross out i, iii and iv, because each one is now used. Heading ii and heading v are still open.
I see that heading ii fits only one sentence in A, not the whole paragraph. A detail is a trap, so I reject it.
moves.mark: Steam engines had pulled coal wagons along the line for decades.

moves.say: I notice heading v is about a bus station, and no paragraph mentions one. So it is wrong too, and I leave it unused.

demo.answer: A: heading i (what happened to the railway line after it closed). B: heading iii (who uses the new walking path). C: heading iv (plans for new trees and wildlife along the route). Heading ii is a detail trap, and heading v is not used.

practice.prompt: Which heading fits paragraph B? Use the steps: read the first and last sentence, then check the whole paragraph. Write the full heading.
practice.text: A: The community garden was started in 2015 by six neighbours who wanted fresh vegetables. Today it has forty plots, and each family pays a small yearly fee. B: Volunteers meet on the first Saturday of every month to repair the fences and water the paths. Many of them say these meetings are the best part of the week. C: Next spring the garden will add a greenhouse, which will let members grow tomatoes in colder months. The money for it has already been raised.
options: How a community garden was started and how it has grown
How volunteers keep the garden in good repair
Plans for a new greenhouse next spring
The cost of buying vegetables in local shops
Which vegetables grow best in cold weather
practice.answer: How volunteers keep the garden in good repair
practice.why: Steps 3 and 4: the first sentence of B says volunteers meet to repair fences, and the last says the meetings matter. The whole paragraph is about their work. The vegetable headings only copy words from A or C.
practice.evidence: Volunteers meet on the first Saturday of every month to repair the fences and water the paths.

practice.prompt: Which heading fits paragraph C? Use the steps. Check that the heading covers the whole paragraph, not only the first or last sentence.
practice.text: A: The school library was once a storeroom for old desks and broken chairs. In 2018 the head teacher turned it into a bright reading room with beanbags and shelves. B: Pupils now borrow more than three hundred books a term, which is double the number from before the change. Teachers say that children who read more often write better stories. C: Not every pupil enjoys reading, however. The school has started a club where students choose the books, so the choice belongs to them. Attendance at the club has grown steadily since its first meeting.
options: How the old storeroom became a reading room
Why some pupils do not enjoy reading
A reading club that lets pupils choose their own books
Why attendance at the club keeps growing
Ways to write better stories in class
practice.answer: A reading club that lets pupils choose their own books
practice.why: Step 7: C opens with a problem, then the rest answers it with the club. 'Why some pupils do not enjoy reading' covers only the first sentence. 'Why attendance keeps growing' covers only the last one.
practice.evidence: The school has started a club where students choose the books, so the choice belongs to them.

tricks: Do the easy paragraphs first. Every heading you cross out makes the hard paragraphs easier.
Read the first and last sentence before anything else. You often find the answer without reading the middle.
There are extra headings on purpose. Do not worry if some are never used.
Look for repeated ideas across the paragraph, not a single word. The main idea is what the paragraph keeps coming back to.
traps: Choosing a heading because one of its words appears in the paragraph. That word may be only a minor detail, so check the main idea.
Choosing a heading that fits only one sentence. The heading must cover the whole paragraph.
Reusing a heading. Each one is used once, so cross it out as soon as you use it.
Reading the whole passage word by word. This wastes time. Use the first and last sentences and skim the rest.

example.text: A: Early cities grew beside rivers. Water was needed for drinking, farming and travel, so people settled where it was easy to find. B: Today, many cities are choosing to keep their old rivers clean. Clean water attracts visitors, and visitors bring money.
example.question: Which heading fits paragraph A? (i) Why rivers matter to modern tourism (ii) The first reasons for building cities near water
walk: Read the first sentence of A: it is about early cities and rivers.
The last sentence says people settled where water was easy to find. This closes the same idea.
Heading (ii) says the same in other words: reasons for building cities near water.
Heading (i) uses a word from the passage, but tourism and money appear in paragraph B, not A. So the answer is ii.

signals.means: The main idea may change here. Check the sentence after it.
A detail follows. Do not choose a heading for an example.
The writer sums up the paragraph, which often matches the heading.
The paragraph is about a process or a list. The heading may mention steps or stages.

checklist: Did I read the headings before the passage?
Does my heading cover the whole paragraph, not one detail?
Did I cross out each heading after using it?
Did I check that the heading is not just a matching word from the text?

title: Matching information
what: You get statements about details, and you decide which paragraph (A, B, C and so on) contains each one. The statements are not in passage order, and a paragraph can be used more than once. These take the longest, so do them last.

steps.do: Read the instructions. Check if a letter can be used more than once.
steps.why: The instructions tell you the rule. Different tests can have different rules.

steps.do: Read all the statements. Underline the key words in each one.
steps.why: You know what to look for in every paragraph, so you read only once.

steps.do: Think of other words for each key word. For example, think of "rise" for "increase".
steps.why: The passage uses a paraphrase, which means the same idea in other words, not your exact words.

steps.do: Skim the paragraphs for the topic of the first statement. Do not read every word yet.
steps.why: You can find the right paragraph by topic first, which is faster than reading it all.

steps.do: Read the likely paragraph carefully. Check that it contains the exact detail, not just the topic.
steps.why: Two paragraphs may share a topic, but only one holds the detail.

steps.do: Write the letter and move to the next statement. If you are stuck, skip it and come back.
steps.why: The statements are not in order, so skipping costs you nothing.

steps.do: Check each answer against the whole statement. Do not avoid a letter just because you used it before.
steps.why: Letters can repeat, so a used letter can still be right.

demo.prompt: Statement: The number of visitors grew after the museum stopped charging for entry. Write the letter of the paragraph, A, B or C. You may use a letter more than once.
demo.text: A: The Lantern Museum opened in 1985 in a former mill. Its first exhibition showed old looms and the wool trade of the town. B: For many years entry cost five pounds, and few families could afford it. Visitor numbers stayed below ten thousand a year. C: In 2019 the museum removed its entry fee and began offering free school tours. Within a year, visitors had more than doubled, and the museum now welcomes around thirty thousand people annually.

moves.say: The rule says a letter can be used more than once. So I will not cross out any letter in this task.
I underline the key words in the statement: grew, and stopped charging. These are my search words.
I think of other words. Stopped charging could mean no longer asking people to pay at the door.
I skim the paragraphs for the topic, which is money at the door. Paragraph B mentions entry cost, so I look there first.
moves.mark: For many years entry cost five pounds, and few families could afford it.

moves.say: I read B carefully. It shows the old price and low numbers, but no growth after a change. So B is not the answer.
moves.mark: Visitor numbers stayed below ten thousand a year.

moves.say: Now I read C closely. The change in 2019 matches stopped charging.
moves.mark: In 2019 the museum removed its entry fee and began offering free school tours.

moves.say: I read the next sentence. Visitors more than doubled, so that matches grew.
moves.mark: Within a year, visitors had more than doubled

moves.say: I write C beside the statement and move on to the next one.
I check the whole statement against C. Stopped charging and grew both match, so the answer is C.
moves.mark: Within a year, visitors had more than doubled

demo.answer: C. The museum removed its entry fee in 2019, and visitors more than doubled within a year.

practice.prompt: Statement: The number of fishing boats fell after fish stocks in the sea declined. Which paragraph, A to D, contains this? Use the steps: find the paraphrase, then the exact detail.
practice.text: A: Hollis Bay has been a fishing port for more than two hundred years. Its harbour wall was built stone by stone by the town's first harbour masters. B: The fishing fleet shrank after 1990, because the cod stocks fell sharply. Many boats were sold, and the young men of the town moved away to find work. Only nine boats now sail from the bay. C: In 2004 the council opened a small seafood school in the old net store. Students learn to fillet fish, cook a simple meal and check the freshness of the catch. Over 500 students have completed the course. D: Tourism has grown steadily since 2010, when a new ferry linked the bay to the city. Visitors come to walk the cliffs and eat in the harbour cafes.
practice.why: Step 3: 'fish stocks declined' means the cod stocks fell, and 'boats fell' means the fleet shrank. Both are in B. Paragraph C mentions fish, but only as a school course, so it is a word-match trap.
practice.evidence: because the cod stocks fell sharply

practice.prompt: Statement: Some young people left the bay to look for work elsewhere. Which paragraph, A to D, contains this? Use the steps.
practice.text: A: Hollis Bay has been a fishing port for more than two hundred years. Its harbour wall was built stone by stone by the town's first harbour masters. B: The fishing fleet shrank after 1990, because the cod stocks fell sharply. Many boats were sold, and the young men of the town moved away to find work. Only nine boats now sail from the bay. C: In 2004 the council opened a small seafood school in the old net store. Students learn to fillet fish, cook a simple meal and check the freshness of the catch. Over 500 students have completed the course. D: Tourism has grown steadily since 2010, when a new ferry linked the bay to the city. Visitors come to walk the cliffs and eat in the harbour cafes.
practice.why: Step 7: B says the young men moved away to find work, the same idea as young people leaving for work. Letters can repeat, so B is right again. D is about visitors, not work.
practice.evidence: the young men of the town moved away to find work

tricks: Do these questions last. They take the most time, so give your time to easier questions first.
Tick the statements you have answered. Paragraphs you have already read are then quicker to scan.
Search for rare words and names first, such as numbers, dates and capital letters. They are easy to find.
When the instructions say you may use any letter more than once, a paragraph you have used can be used again. Do not rule it out.
traps: Expecting the answers in order. They are not, so do each statement separately.
Choosing a paragraph because it shares a word with the statement. Check the full meaning instead.
Looking for the exact words of the statement. The passage paraphrases, so look for the idea.
Spending too long on one statement. Skip it and return if you have time.

example.text: A: The shop opened in 1990 and sold only books. B: By 2005 the owner had added a cafe because customers wanted somewhere to sit. C: Today, half of its income comes from online sales.
example.question: Which paragraph mentions a reason for a change to the shop? Write the correct letter, A-C.
example.evidence: because customers wanted somewhere to sit
walk: The key words are reason and change. Another word for reason is because.
Paragraph A describes the start, not a change. Paragraph C gives a fact about income, with no reason.
Paragraph B says the owner added a cafe because customers wanted somewhere to sit.
That is a change and its reason, so the answer is B.

signals.means: A reason or cause. Useful for statements about reasons.
An example. Useful for statements about examples.
A contrast or a different view.
Easy to scan for. A statement with a figure is quick to find.

checklist: Did I check whether a letter can be used more than once?
Did I underline the key words and think of other words for them?
Does the paragraph contain the exact detail, not only the topic?
Did I skip hard statements and come back to them?

title: Matching features
what: You get a list of features, such as people, places or theories, and a set of statements. You decide which feature each statement is about. A feature can be used more than once. The statements are not in passage order.

steps.do: Read the instructions. Check if you can use an option more than once.
steps.why: The rule changes how you cross out options.

steps.do: Find the features in the passage. Underline each name or theory every time it appears.
steps.why: You make a map of the passage, so you can go straight to the right place.

steps.do: Read each statement. Underline the key words and think of other words for them.
steps.why: The passage uses a paraphrase, which means the same idea in other words.

steps.do: Find the key words of the statement near an underlined name. Read that sentence closely.
steps.why: The statement is usually in the same sentence as the name, or the next one.

steps.do: Check the verb of opinion, such as "claims", "denies" or "suggests". Make sure it matches the statement.
steps.why: Two people may discuss one topic but disagree, so the verb decides who is right.

steps.do: Write the letter of the feature. If a pronoun like "he" or "she" is used, check which name it means.
steps.why: A pronoun can hide the name, which causes wrong answers.

steps.do: Move on. If you are stuck, skip the statement and return.
steps.why: The statements are not in order, so skipping costs nothing.

demo.prompt: Features: A Ms Okafor, B Mr Lindqvist, C Dr Patel. Statement: Someone thinks the road will damage the valley's animals. Write A, B or C. You may use a letter more than once.
demo.text: Ms Okafor argues that the new road will bring jobs to the region. Mr Lindqvist, however, doubts that the road will bring any real benefit, and he fears it will harm the wildlife in the valley. Dr Patel suggests that a tunnel would be better than a road across the hills.

moves.say: I read the rule. A feature can be used more than once, so I will not cross out any letter yet.
I underline each name in the passage. Names are my map, so I find them first.
moves.mark: Ms Okafor argues that the new road will bring jobs to the region.

moves.say: I see Mr Lindqvist and Dr Patel in the next two sentences. I underline each name every time it shows up.
moves.mark: Mr Lindqvist, however, doubts that the road will bring any real benefit, and he fears it will harm the wildlife in the valley.

moves.say: I think of other words. Damage could mean harm, and animals could mean wildlife.
The road is a key word, so I check the sentence near each name. Ms Okafor's sentence is about road jobs, not harm.
moves.mark: Ms Okafor argues that the new road will bring jobs to the region.

moves.say: I see that Mr Lindqvist's sentence has the verb fears. A fear that the road will harm nature matches the statement.
moves.mark: he fears it will harm the wildlife in the valley

moves.say: I check Dr Patel's verb: suggests, and the claim is that a tunnel is better. That is not a claim of harm, so I rule Dr Patel out.
moves.mark: Dr Patel suggests that a tunnel would be better than a road across the hills.

moves.say: 'He' in this sentence means Mr Lindqvist, because his name opens it. So the fear belongs to B.
moves.mark: he fears it will harm the wildlife in the valley

moves.say: I write B, Mr Lindqvist, beside the statement. B is my answer.
I check the whole statement. The opinion verb fears matches the idea of damage, so B is correct.
moves.mark: he fears it will harm the wildlife in the valley

demo.answer: B (Mr Lindqvist). He fears the road will harm the wildlife; the other two speakers do not say this.

practice.prompt: Claim: Working from home saves time and makes staff happier. Which speaker agrees? Use the steps: find each name, then check the opinion verb. Write the full name.
practice.text: Ruth Calder believes that people work best in an office, where they can share ideas quickly. Tom Amari, by contrast, claims that home working saves time and makes staff happier. Nadia Ruiz says the best solution is a mix, with two days at home and three in the office.
practice.why: Step 5: 'claims' is an opinion verb, and Tom's claim matches the statement word for word in meaning. Ruth prefers the office and Nadia wants a mix, so neither agrees with the claim.
practice.evidence: Tom Amari, by contrast, claims that home working saves time and makes staff happier.

practice.prompt: Claim: The railway was profitable for a long time before it closed. Which speaker holds this view? Use the steps: watch for a speaker who opposes the idea, and check the verb. Write the full name.
practice.text: Dr Hughes insists that the old railway was never profitable, and says it should have closed decades earlier. Priya Shah disagrees: she believes the railway was profitable for thirty years, until a bus company undercut it. Ben Walsh, who worked on the line for years, says that closing it was a mistake, and that the council decided too quickly.
practice.why: Step 5: Dr Hughes says the railway was never profitable, the opposite of the claim. Ben Walsh judges the closing decision, not the profit. Only Priya's verb 'believes' fits a profitable period of thirty years.
practice.evidence: she believes the railway was profitable for thirty years, until a bus company undercut it

tricks: Underline every name in the passage first. The names are your map, so the rest is quick.
Look for opinion verbs: argues, believes, claims, suggests, doubts. They link a person to an idea.
A feature can be used more than once, and some may not be used at all.
Find the names in the passage first, then read the statement and match its idea to the right name.
traps: Choosing the first name you see near the topic. Check who actually said or did it.
Ignoring the verb. Someone who "doubts" an idea is not someone who "supports" it.
Missing a pronoun. "He" or "she" may point to a name in the sentence before.
Expecting the answers in order. They are not, so do each statement separately.

example.text: Dr Hale argues that children learn language mainly by copying adults. Professor Reyes disagrees and says that children are born with a natural ability for grammar.
example.question: Which person says children have a built-in talent for grammar? A Dr Hale B Professor Reyes
example.evidence: children are born with a natural ability for grammar
walk: The key words are built-in talent. Another way to say this is born with a natural ability.
Dr Hale is linked to copying adults, which is a different idea.
Professor Reyes disagrees and says children are born with a natural ability for grammar.
The meaning matches the statement, so the answer is B.

signals.means: Verbs that show a person gives an opinion.
Verbs that show a person opposes an idea.
Names the source of an idea, which links a person to a statement.
A pronoun that points back to a name. Check who it means.

checklist: Did I check whether an option can be used more than once?
Did I underline every name or theory in the passage first?
Does the verb of opinion match the statement?
Did I check who a pronoun like "he" or "she" means?

title: Matching sentence endings
what: You get the first half of several sentences and a list of possible endings. You choose the ending that completes each sentence correctly, using the passage. There are more endings than sentence starts, and each ending is used once.

steps.do: Read the sentence starts. They follow the order of the passage, so the first start is near the beginning.
steps.why: The order lets you search forward through the text without going back.

steps.do: Underline the key words in each start. Find that place in the passage.
steps.why: The key words take you straight to the right sentence.

steps.do: Read the endings. Rule out those that break the grammar when joined to the start.
steps.why: Grammar removes wrong endings fast, before you think about meaning.

steps.do: Read the passage near the key words. Decide what it says, then look for that meaning in the endings.
steps.why: The ending is a paraphrase, which means the same idea in other words.

steps.do: Pick the ending that matches the meaning. Do not pick one just because it uses words from the passage.
steps.why: A wrong ending may copy the passage words but change the meaning.

steps.do: Cross out each ending once you use it. Move to the next start.
steps.why: Each ending is used once, so every cross removes a choice.

steps.do: Read each finished sentence. Confirm it with a line from the passage.
steps.why: A line in the passage proves your answer is right, not a guess.

demo.prompt: Sentence start: The bridge was closed for six months because... Endings: A engineers found cracks in its arches. B the council wanted to repair the arches. C to find the cracks in its arches. D the arches, which were built in 1900. Which ending, A to D, completes the sentence?
demo.text: The old bridge was closed in March for six months. During a routine check, engineers found serious cracks in its arches. The council said that the decision was about safety, not money.

moves.say: I read the sentence start first. Starts follow the passage order, but the endings do not, so I do not expect them in order.
I underline the key words: bridge, closed, six months. The start ends with 'because', so I need a reason.
I check grammar first. After 'because' I need a full clause, so option C, starting with 'to', fails.
I see that option D has no main verb. 'The arches, which were built in 1900' is not a full clause, so it fails too.
I read the passage near the key words. It says a check found damage, so the reason is about the cracks.
moves.mark: During a routine check, engineers found serious cracks in its arches.

moves.say: Option B copies arches and repair, but the passage gives safety as the reason, not repairs. So I reject B.
moves.mark: The council said that the decision was about safety, not money.

moves.say: I see that option A matches the passage line. B copies more words, but its meaning does not fit, so I pick A by meaning.
moves.mark: During a routine check, engineers found serious cracks in its arches.

moves.say: I write A beside the start and cross it out from the list, because each ending is used once.
I read the full sentence and confirm it with a line from the passage. The line proves that A is right.
moves.mark: During a routine check, engineers found serious cracks in its arches.

demo.answer: A. The bridge was closed for six months because engineers found cracks in its arches.

practice.prompt: Sentence start: The organisers moved the stalls indoors because... Which ending completes it? Use the steps: grammar first, then meaning, then a line from the passage. Write the full ending.
practice.text: The village festival is usually held on the green. This year, however, heavy rain soaked the grass on the morning of the event. The organisers moved the stalls into the village hall, where everything could stay dry. Visitors said the hall felt crowded, but most of them stayed until the evening. Next year the committee plans to build a covered area on the green, so that the festival can go ahead in any weather.
options: heavy rain had soaked the grass
visitors said the hall felt crowded
most visitors stayed until the evening
the festival can go ahead in any weather
practice.answer: heavy rain had soaked the grass
practice.why: Step 3: 'to keep everything dry' is true in the passage, but it cannot follow 'because', so only grammar rules it out. The passage says heavy rain soaked the grass, which is the reason.
practice.evidence: heavy rain soaked the grass on the morning of the event

practice.prompt: Sentence start: Visitors said the hall felt crowded, but... Use the steps: grammar first, then meaning, then a line from the passage. Write the full ending.
practice.text: The village festival is usually held on the green. This year, however, heavy rain soaked the grass on the morning of the event. The organisers moved the stalls into the village hall, where everything could stay dry. Visitors said the hall felt crowded, but most of them stayed until the evening. Next year the committee plans to build a covered area on the green, so that the festival can go ahead in any weather.
options: heavy rain had soaked the grass
visitors said the hall felt crowded
most visitors stayed until the evening
the festival can go ahead in any weather
practice.answer: most visitors stayed until the evening
practice.why: Step 3: 'but to keep everything dry' fails grammar, but two other endings pass. Step 4: the passage says most of them stayed, which fits the 'but'. The other two are real details that do not fit the contrast.
practice.evidence: but most of them stayed until the evening

tricks: The sentence starts are in passage order, but the endings are not. Do not expect the answers in order.
Check grammar first. If the start ends with "to", the ending must begin with a verb.
There are extra endings on purpose, so some will not be used.
Cross out each ending as you use it. The last choices are easy.
traps: Choosing an ending because it repeats words from the passage. Check that the meaning is the same.
Ignoring the grammar. A true idea still cannot be joined to a start that does not fit.
